title: Rescue amputee returns to duty
description: Senior Airman Kevin Greene, (Melbourne, Florida resident; Brooklyn, New York native), an Air Force Reserve amputee with 920th Rescue Wing, returned to work Aug. 6, 2017 after more than two years of being inactive. Greene, who lost a portion of his left leg in a motorcycle accident on Dec. 17, 2014, is the first and only Air Force Reserve amputee to serve at Patrick AFB.

transcript.text: (sirens wailing)
- When I woke up in the hospital,
I hear in the background, people crying hysterically,
just family praying.
The next thing I see, a little bit after that,
shortly after I woke up, is the doctor walk in
and tell me everything is, I'm okay.
My brain is fine, no spinal damage,
and I asked him what happened.
He told me that I got a pretty severe motorcycle accident.
Then, I asked him how severe
because I'm looking at my hands, I'm looking at my body,
I felt fine, I felt good.
He told me that they amputated my left foot,
so that's when things got surreal for me.
(soft music)
^- I'd like to think that he had a strong support group,
^not only from his civilian friends and family,
but his military friends and family
that just try to come out and see him
and speak to him and show him some love.
(soft music)
- I would say my support system,
that really kept me motivated
to continue with rehab, to continue with the process
because I stopped trusting the process.
(determined music)
I just tell that person that's trying to come back
from an injury or whatever,
just keep working on yourself while you wait
and be positive with it.
(determined music)
^- He is a natural at getting those children
^to open up to him.
One of our non-verbal kids, first thing they noticed was
Mr. Kevin's leg's a little different than everyone.
Instead of being embarrassed or taken back by that,
he owns it, and I think that's what makes Kevin shine.
(joyful music)
- So excited to be in the Air Force uniform,
and to have the opportunity to test again.
(triumphant music)
- A lot of people would have given in to depression,
to despair, to the loss.
He didn't.
He's a driven person.
He went through all these hoops, denials,
the Air Force, saying that no, you can't serve.
And he showed them that no, I can.
I'm not limited.
I can do the same job.
I'm glad he proved that point, and the Air Force listened.
- Before I got hurt, I was just career driven,
and then after I got hurt, I started appreciating things
like people who know when you get the opportunity
to say what you want to say.
You never know when you'll see that person again.
Go outta your way to say hello, see how they're doin'.
It's selfless.
It's the best way to go.
